        with patch("builtins.open") as m:
            route()
            m.assert_has_calls(
                [
                    call("capture_pipeline.yml", "w+"),

Q: What is the difference between "is None" and "== None" A:

Integer Caching, is and ==

I'm going to assume you're really asking about is and == rather than merely the None aspect, as the first two are the source of a lot of errors that a programmer might think is due merely to None.

Something I haven't seen mentioned in these answers is that certain commonly and frequently used values (specifically -5 to +256) are cached/preloaded by Python to be mapped to automatically created objects, created upon program startup. Python is using "Integer Caching".

Both 256 is 256 and 256 == 256 evaluate to True.

  • 256 is 256 is treated as PtrToPreexistingGLOBALObj256 == PtrToPreexistingGLOBALObj256 -> True.
  • This makes sense. Upon randomly asking anybody, they would likely guess that both methods should produce the same output.

However, 257 is 257 is different than 257 == 257.

  • 257 is 257 is treated as PtrTo(CreateNewInteger(257)) == PtrTo(CreateNewInteger(257)) -> False
  • 257 == 257 is checking the actual content's value rather than just quickly checking the object's memory address, == doing something like (CreateNewInteger(257)).__value__ == (CreateNewInteger(257)).__value__ -> True.

So, if you want to compare two pieces of data (their actual values, not their memory addresses) *and* are okay with the `==` operator potentially being overloaded by another class that you don't know about, you should use `==` instead of `is`.

Important Note: Most of my syntax in this answer is pseudocode, not actual code.

Info source: Daily Coding Professor on a YouTube Short named "Why "is" is NOT the same as "=="" as of Feb 23, 2026

Q: pip upgrade uninstalled itself A:

If anyone is using Ubuntu and has lost pip after running pip install --upgrade pip Due to some permission errors, you can reinstall pip back like this:

sudo apt install python3-pip

Q: googleMobileAds no-fill - Request Error: No ad to show A:

I totally get it! That [googleMobileAds/no-fill] error is a classic headache, your code is likely solid and it’s probably just a matter of waiting on Google.

Why are you seeing "No Fill"?

It’s not necessarily a bug; it just means the request was successful, but AdMob didn't have an ad to show you at that exact moment. This usually happens because:

  • Inventory Availability: AdMob doesn’t guarantee an ad 100% of the time. Especially with new apps or new ad units, it takes time for demand to catch up.

  • App Approval Delay: Even if your app is already approved, ad serving can take several days to a week to stabilize and show live ads consistently.

  • Targeting Settings: If you’ve added strict keywords or restricted many categories, you might be narrowing your chances of getting a fill.

  • Geography: Fill rates vary significantly by region. Testing in certain countries might result in fewer available ads.

Quick Double-Check List

To give yourself some peace of mind that your integration is correct, verify these points:

  1. Test IDs: Always confirm that test ads load correctly. If test ads work, your integration is fine—the issue is purely inventory.

  2. Ad Unit IDs: Make sure you’re using the correct format (ca-app-pub-XXXX/XXXX) for banners and interstitials respectively.

  3. Initialization: You already confirmed mobileAds().initialize() is running, which is the most important step.

  4. Real Device Testing: You're doing it right—simulators often struggle to show live ads, so stick to physical devices.

Recommended Next Steps

  • Give it Time: AdMob often takes a few extra days to start serving live ads after an app is approved.

  • Stick to Test Ads: Keep using them until you start seeing live inventory appear consistently.

  • Loosen Targeting: Remove or broaden any keyword filters to maximize your potential fill rate.

  • Check your Dashboard: Log into AdMob to ensure there are no policy violations or temporary serving limits on your account (common for new developers).

Q: Right usage of 2>&1 | tee or | tee with powershell A:

In both editions of PowerShell, redirecting stderr lines from an external program to PowerShell's success output stream via 2>&1 wraps those lines in [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord] instances.

In Windows PowerShell, the legacy, ships-with-Windows, Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1, these instances render like PowerShell errors, which is why you're seeing the red, multiline output (by contrast, without the redirection, the stderr lines would be passed through to the console, as-is, without coloring).

A simple workaround is to convert these objects to strings explicitly, which outputs the original lines (PSv3+ syntax; built-in alias % for ForEach-Object used for brevity):

... 2>&1 | % ToString | Tee-Object output.txt

Alternatively, more concisely, using the built-in oss function (which is a wrapper around Out-String -Stream):

# Note: Use Out-String -Stream directly in lieu of oss for better performance.
... 2>&1 | oss | Tee-Object output.txt

Note:

  • These workarounds are no longer strictly necessary in the install-on-demand, cross-platform PowerShell (Core) 7 edition, where even wrapped stderr lines now consistently render just as strings.

  • However, when redirected-to-the-success-stream stderr lines (which, as noted, become [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord] instances) print to the console (terminal) - as opposed to to a file with >, Out-File, or Tee-Object or to a string with Out-String[1] - they still print in red (albeit just as text, not in the multiline, pseudo error format used by Windows PowerShell); for instance, try
    cmd /c 'echo stdout & echo stderr >&2' 2>&1

  • To avoid colored redirected-to-the-success-stream stderr lines in terminal output in PowerShell (Core) 7, you have two options:

    • Use one of the workarounds above, as in Windows PowerShell, i.e. force conversion to strings.
      This is also the technique to use if you want to programmatically process all output lines from an external program as text, in memory, whether from stdout or stderr, without relying on implicit type conversions.

    • (Possibly temporarily) use the $PSStyle preference variable to set $PSStyle.OutputRendering = 'PlainText'.
      Conversely, use 'Ansi' if you want to preserve coloring even when printing to a file, using > / Out-File or Tee-Object; note that the resulting files will have embedded VT/ANSI escape sequences[1]

[1] What implicit to-console (to-host) output and > as well as said cmdlets have in common is that PowerShell's rich for-display output formatting system is involved, whose coloring behavior is guided by the value of $PSStyle.OutputRendering, which defaults to 'Host', which means that coloring is by default only applied when printing to the host (console), not also when relaying output via the pipeline or sending it to a file.
'PlainText' instructs the formatting system to never apply coloring, even when printing to the host, whereas 'Ansi' always applies coloring.
